en: The *Praṇavakalpa*, among all the fundamental works composed by the venerable Śrīmad Ānandatīrtha Bhagavatpāda. Salutations to Śrī Lakṣmī-Hayagrīva, who is identical with Śrī Hanumān, Abhimanyu, Madhva, Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, and Vedavyāsa.
Having offered oblations of clarified butter according to the rules while properly reciting the Puruṣasūkta,
and having granted fearlessness to all beings, one who is dispassionate should go forth as a renunciant toward Lord Hari.
Having heard the pure Bhāgavata, one should go for refuge to a teacher;
to him who says, "O Blessed One, teach me Brahman," the guru should speak the Supreme.
Uttering the three stars (Tāraka-mantra) three times into his right ear,
the wise preceptor should then recite the sage, the meter, and the deity in their proper order.
The Antaryāmī, the Gāyatrī, and the Paramātman, in this sequence,
are Viśva, Taijasa, Prājña, and Turya— the deities of the imperishable syllables.
Kṛṣṇa, Rāma, Nṛsiṃha, Varāha, Viṣṇu, Parañjyotis, Parabrahman, and Vāsudeva— these are the names in sequence.
Having thus spoken of the deities corresponding to the letters beginning with 'a' and ending with 'śānta' and 'atiśānta', the true guru should then explain that meditation to the disciple.
In the center of the eight-petaled heart-lotus is a pedestal situated within the sun, moon, and fire;
upon that, in the middle of the lotus, resides the stainless Nārāyaṇa.
He is always like the rising sun, incomparable in splendor,
and possesses a form that surpasses even a thousand suns in brilliance.
With the soles of his feet exceedingly red, resplendent with rows of shining nails,
with rounded calves and rounded knees, and possessing thighs like the trunks of elephants, he was the supreme lord.
Resplendent in yellow garments with a golden girdle fastened upon his broad hips,
he possesses a deep navel, three beautiful folds of skin on his abdomen, and a well-rounded waist.
He had a broad chest, with the radiant Kaustubha gem resting upon his unbound neck;
he wore a forest garland and was adorned with necklaces, the Vaijayantī, and other ornaments.
He has four arms, broad and long, endowed with the conch, discus, mace, and lotus; his eyes are like blooming lotuses, and he wears shimmering makara-shaped earrings.
His lotus-face possessed a splendor exceeding ten thousand full moons;
he had beautiful eyebrows and a lovely forehead, with his hair bound by a diadem.
He who pacifies all suffering without remainder, whose smile is eternal bliss and purity,
and who likewise [created] the primordial lords of the universe, such as Kṛṣṇa and others, who are thus eternal.
Therefore, [one should meditate] constantly upon those who are indeed non-different from Viṣṇu, the Supreme Self,
whose hands are raised granting boons and fearlessness, and whose nature is solely eternal bliss.
Having spoken thus, the guru should then cause him to perform meditation and take an oath three times, saying: "I shall never abandon Viṣṇu nor the Vaiṣṇavas. (16)
Nor would I, even after death, contemplate any equality with other deities, nor identity with Hari, nor even unity with those who profess monism. (17)
O great sage, I might somehow come into contact with those who preach equality, or with those who revile it, or even with those who revile its proponents. (18)
When the oath has been thus performed, having placed his lotus-hand upon [the other's] head and having crossed over the cycle of worldly existence, one becomes happy and dear to Hari.
Liberated from all sufferings and the like, having attained proximity to Viṣṇu whose singular nature is eternal bliss, he remains there possessed of devotion to Hari.
Always possessing devotion toward other deities while remembering the hierarchy and the supreme excellence of Viṣṇu, one should speak thus and shall always be happy.
"Neither unity with Viṣṇu in liberation, nor even equality among the liberated ones, should you remember"—having said this, he should instruct them in the rules of conduct (samayas). || 22 ||
O child, you must constantly perform the worship of Hari, as well as recitation, meditation, and dedication; indeed, the recitation should consist of three thousand repetitions.

That which is declared as the middling [repetition] of the Praṇava consists of one thousand; that which is inferior consists of two thousand; and that which exceeds three thousand is remembered as the highest repetition (japa). || 24 ||
Meditating on yourself as the reflection and Janārdana as the original image,
and constantly meditating [on Him], O child, perform worship perpetually.
Or else, being composed, you should recite with the *praṇava* either mentally or with flowers, as well as other Vaiṣṇava mantras, preceded by devotion. (26)
Listen to the Vaiṣṇava scripture, always intent upon the true meaning of the Vedas;
listen at all times to the Vedas along with their mantras and Upaniṣads.
Furthermore, having correctly determined the true meaning of the Itihāsas, Purāṇas, and likewise the Pañcarātra through the Brahma-sūtras according to reality,
always establish the supreme excellence of Viṣṇu.
Thus ends the *Praṇavakalpa* composed by the venerable teacher Śrīmad Ānandatīrtha Bhagavatpāda.
Thus ends the ritual manual for the Praṇava.
May this be offered unto Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
